questions.question: A Spring Boot pod is stuck in `Pending` state and not scheduling — how do you debug it?
questions.title: Debugging `Pending` Pods: Scheduling Failures in Kubernetes
questions.direct_answer: Run `kubectl describe pod` first — the `Events` section almost always shows the exact reason. Common causes: (1) **Insufficient resources** — no node has the requested CPU/memory; fix by adding nodes (Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter) or lowering requests, (2) **Affinity / taints / topology spread constraints** that exclude all nodes, (3) **PersistentVolumeClaim unbound** because no StorageClass or no PV matches, (4) **No nodes match `nodeSelector`** labels, (5) **ImagePullBackOff-like but for scheduling** when node has taint and pod lacks toleration, (6) **Quota exceeded** on namespace. Walk the stack: events → node capacity → PVC status → affinity/taints → quota.

interviewer_intent.testing: Systematic debugging skill — Google SRE-style 'give me a hypothesis per data point' reasoning
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping to 'restart the pod' or 'add more nodes' before reading `kubectl describe` events; assuming Pending always means resource shortage
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain scheduler's Filter+Score phases, how to read `FailedScheduling` events, PVC WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode, topologySpreadConstraints DoNotSchedule vs ScheduleAnyway, and ResourceQuota vs LimitRange differences

sections.title: The Diagnostic Instinct: `Pending` Means the Scheduler Cannot Place This Pod
sections.content:
A pod in `Pending` is a pod **the scheduler has not yet placed on any node**. It is NOT a container crash or image pull failure — those are `CrashLoopBackOff` and `ImagePullBackOff` respectively, which happen AFTER scheduling. `Pending` means the pod is sitting in the scheduler's queue with no node satisfying its constraints.

The Kubernetes scheduler runs two phases per pending pod:

1. **Filter (Predicates)** — which nodes are candidates? Eliminates nodes with insufficient resources, taints the pod can't tolerate, affinity violations, label mismatches.
2. **Score (Priorities)** — which of the remaining nodes is best? Picks one.

If Filter returns zero nodes, the pod stays Pending with a `FailedScheduling` event explaining why. **Your job**: read that event and walk backward.

The top five root causes in production order:

1. **Insufficient resources** — every node is too full for the pod's requests.
2. **PVC not bound** — pod waits for storage, storage waits for pod (with WaitForFirstConsumer).
3. **Taints without tolerations** — newly tainted nodes exclude pods lacking matching tolerations.
4. **Topology / affinity constraints** too strict — spread rules or anti-affinity prevent placement.
5. **ResourceQuota exceeded** on namespace — no quota left for the new pod.

A 15-second `kubectl describe pod` reveals which one it is.

sections.title: The Debugging Decision Tree
sections.content:
Walk the stack top-down from `Events` to root cause.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Start[Pod Pending\nkubectl describe pod] --> Events{Events section}
    Events -->|Insufficient cpu/memory| Res[Resource shortage path]
    Events -->|FailedScheduling\nnode\(s\) had untolerated taint| Taint[Taint/Toleration path]
    Events -->|FailedScheduling\nno match for node selector| Sel[nodeSelector / affinity path]
    Events -->|FailedScheduling\npod has unbound PVCs| PVC[Storage path]
    Events -->|exceeded quota| Q[ResourceQuota path]
    Events -->|didnt match pod topology spread constraints| TSC[Topology spread path]

    Res --> R1[kubectl top nodes]
    R1 --> R2{Cluster has headroom?}
    R2 -->|No| R3[Add nodes\nKarpenter/CA]
    R2 -->|Yes, scheduler wont fit| R4[Check pod requests\nvs node allocatable]

    Taint --> T1[kubectl describe node | grep Taint]
    T1 --> T2[Add toleration or remove taint]

    Sel --> S1[kubectl get nodes --show-labels]
    S1 --> S2[Fix nodeSelector or label the node]

    PVC --> P1[kubectl get pvc]
    P1 --> P2{Status}
    P2 -->|Pending| P3[Check StorageClass\nCSI driver / zone]
    P2 -->|WaitForFirstConsumer| P4[Expected - binds when pod schedules\nbut pod cant schedule yet -> other cause]

    Q --> Q1[kubectl describe resourcequota -n ns]
```

The `Events` section is the compass. Every branch below it is verifiable with one `kubectl` command.

sections.title: Step 1: `kubectl describe pod` and Read the Events Section
sections.content:
Always start here. The scheduler writes its failure reason as an Event on the pod.

```bash
kubectl describe pod order-svc-7d8b-abc -n prod
# ...
# Events:
#   Type     Reason            From               Message
#   ----     ------            ----               -------
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/6 nodes are available:
#     3 Insufficient cpu,
#     2 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu},
#     1 Insufficient memory.
#     preemption: 0/6 nodes are available: 6 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
```

**How to read this:** the scheduler checked 6 nodes. Each failed a specific predicate:

- 3 nodes: not enough free CPU for this pod's `requests.cpu`.
- 2 nodes: tainted `dedicated: gpu` and pod has no matching toleration.
- 1 node: not enough free memory.

Total: zero nodes pass Filter → `Pending` forever until something changes.

**If you see `FailedScheduling` with `pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims`** — the pod references a PVC that hasn't bound yet; go to Step 3.

**If you see nothing in Events** after many minutes — the scheduler may itself be down or a CRD admission webhook is blocking the pod. Check `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` for kube-scheduler health, and `kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations` for webhooks that might be failing.

**`kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n prod`** gives a namespace-wide view if you want to see whether many pods share the same scheduling problem.

sections.title: Step 2: Resource Shortage — The Most Common Cause
sections.content:
If Events say `Insufficient cpu` or `Insufficient memory`, verify and decide between adding capacity or reducing requests.

```bash
kubectl top nodes                           # live usage
kubectl describe node NODE | grep -A5 Allocated
# Allocated resources:
#   Resource           Requests       Limits
#   cpu                3700m (92%)    6200m
#   memory             11Gi (73%)     14Gi
```

**Key concept: requests vs usage.** The scheduler places pods based on **requests**, not actual usage. A node at 40% CPU usage can still reject new pods if requests already total 95% of allocatable. The scheduler is pessimistic — it reserves what pods requested.

**Pod requests:**

```bash
kubectl get pod order-svc-... -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources.requests}'
# {"cpu":"2","memory":"4Gi"}
```

If requests are oversized vs actual need, lower them — this is a VPA-in-`Off`-mode opportunity to get right-sized recommendations.

**If requests are legitimate:**

- **Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter** should provision a new node — check its logs: `kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/cluster-autoscaler`. Common issues: scaling group hit max size, no instance type in the pool fits the pod shape, IAM permissions for scaling.
- **Manual scale** as a fix: raise ASG max / MachinePool max, or add a Karpenter NodePool with a larger instance family.
- **Karpenter `karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt` annotations** on critical pods can prevent consolidation churn but also block node replacement.

**Pod density per node.** On AWS VPC CNI, small instances (t3.small has 11 pod limit) fill up by pod count before CPU. `kubectl describe node | grep 'Non-terminated Pods'` shows count vs capacity.

sections.title: Step 3: PVC Unbound, Taints/Tolerations, and Topology Spread
sections.content:
**PVC unbound.** The pod references a PVC that is not yet `Bound`.

```bash
kubectl get pvc -n prod
# NAME         STATUS    STORAGECLASS   VOLUME   AGE
# order-data   Pending   gp3                     5m

kubectl describe pvc order-data -n prod
# Events:
#   Warning  ProvisioningFailed ... no persistent volumes available for this claim and
#                                  no storage class is set
```

**Common fixes:**

- Set `storageClassName` on the PVC or have a default `StorageClass` (`kubectl get sc` — look for `(default)`).
- Wrong zone: pod is scheduled to zone `us-east-1a`, PV was provisioned in `us-east-1b`. With `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` on the StorageClass, binding waits until the scheduler picks a node — then provisions in that zone. This is the correct mode for multi-AZ clusters.
- CSI driver not healthy: `kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi`.
- Quota on storage: `kubectl describe resourcequota | grep storage`.

**Taints and tolerations.**

```bash
kubectl describe node NODE | grep -A1 Taints
# Taints: dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule
```

Pods lacking a matching toleration are excluded. Either remove the taint (if unintended) or add a toleration:

```yaml
spec:
  tolerations:
    - key: dedicated
      operator: Equal
      value: gpu
      effect: NoSchedule
```

**Common surprise:** nodes get auto-tainted when `NotReady` or under memory pressure (`node.kubernetes.io/not-ready`, `node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure`). If all nodes are tainted like this, your cluster is unhealthy — investigate kubelet / network / disk.

**Topology spread constraints.**

```yaml
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels: {app: order-svc}
```

`DoNotSchedule` means if the spread is violated (e.g., 2 pods in AZ-a, 0 in AZ-b, 0 in AZ-c), the scheduler blocks. Relax to `ScheduleAnyway` or adjust `maxSkew`. Google / Uber / Shopify use spread constraints heavily for AZ / host diversity; misconfigured spread is a classic Pending cause during rolling updates.

**Affinity / anti-affinity.** Pod anti-affinity with `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` saying "no two pods on the same node" limits placement to nodes without an existing pod. If you have 5 replicas and 4 nodes, the 5th stays Pending forever.

**ResourceQuota.**

```bash
kubectl describe resourcequota -n prod
# Resource              Used     Hard
# requests.cpu          15       16
# requests.memory       30Gi     32Gi
# pods                  48       50
```

Near-full quotas block new pods with `exceeded quota` in Events. Either raise the quota or free pods. LimitRange (per-pod min/max) vs ResourceQuota (namespace total) — different tools; Quota is the one that blocks scheduling counts.

sections.title: Production Playbook: Ordering, Tooling, and Preventive Measures
sections.content:
**15-second triage:**

```bash
kubectl describe pod $POD -n $NS | tail -30     # Events
kubectl get pvc -n $NS                           # any Pending?
kubectl top nodes                                # headroom?
kubectl get events -n $NS --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
```

**5-minute deeper dive:**

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node NODE | grep -E 'Taints|Allocatable|Allocated'
kubectl get pods -n $NS -o wide                  # distribution
kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/cluster-autoscaler --tail=100
kubectl get resourcequota -n $NS
```

**Tools that save time:**

- **`kubectl-debug-scheduler`** / scheduler verbose logs (`--v=5`) — see exact filter decisions per node.
- **`kubectl events`** (1.25+) — richer than `kubectl get events`.
- **`k9s` or `Lens`** — interactive event viewing.
- **Prometheus alerts:** `kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Pending"} > 5m` — anything Pending more than 5 minutes is an incident.
- **Metrics:** `scheduler_pending_pods`, `scheduler_framework_extension_point_duration_seconds` — scheduler internal health.

**Preventive measures:**

- **Set resource requests based on VPA recommendations**, not guesses — oversized requests cause unnecessary Pending.
- **PodDisruptionBudget + minReplicas ≥ 2** prevents rolling updates from pinning a lone pod unable to find a new home.
- **Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter with sensible bounds** — max node count, spot diversification, instance family list.
- **`priorityClassName` on critical workloads** — high priority pods preempt lower-priority pods if no node has room, avoiding Pending for the most important services.
- **Test topology spread changes in staging** — DoNotSchedule bugs show up only during rollouts when distribution becomes tight.
- **Avoid `requiredDuringScheduling...` anti-affinity with too strict keys** — often ScheduleAnyway or topology spread is more flexible.

**Escalation pattern:**

1. Single pod Pending — look at pod spec / target node constraints.
2. All new pods in namespace Pending — check Quota, StorageClass, default LimitRange.
3. All new pods cluster-wide Pending — check scheduler health, CNI/CSI driver, node readiness.
4. Pods Pending during rollout only — PDB vs HPA interaction, surge capacity, topology spread tightness.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pending = scheduler cannot place** — not a crash, not an image pull; the pod is stuck in the queue.
- **`kubectl describe pod` Events section is the compass** — it says EXACTLY which predicate failed on which nodes.
- **Scheduler uses `requests`, not actual usage** — a node at 30% CPU usage can still reject pods if requests total 95% of allocatable.
- **PVC with `WaitForFirstConsumer` binds only after a pod is placed** — multi-AZ safe; but if other constraints block scheduling, PVC stays Pending in lock-step.
- **Auto-taints from NotReady / memory-pressure** exclude pods cluster-wide — if every new pod is Pending with taint reasons, your nodes are unhealthy.
- **`DoNotSchedule` topology spread is strict** — classic Pending cause during scale events; switch to `ScheduleAnyway` or adjust `maxSkew`.
- **ResourceQuota blocks scheduling when exceeded** — `kubectl describe resourcequota` shows usage vs limit.
- **PriorityClass preemption** — high-priority pods evict lower ones to schedule; plan priority classes per workload tier.
- **Prometheus alert on Pending duration > 5 min** catches slow/silent scheduling issues before they pile up.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When a pod is stuck in Pending, my first move is always `kubectl describe pod` and I read the Events section. The scheduler writes its failure reason there — it will literally say why each node was rejected.

**Walking the decision tree**
- The most common reason is resource shortage — "0/6 nodes are available: Insufficient cpu". I check `kubectl top nodes` for headroom and compare requests to allocatable; then check the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter logs to see why it isn't adding nodes.
- A key concept: the scheduler uses requests, not actual usage. A node at 30% CPU usage can still reject pods if committed requests already total 95% of allocatable — the scheduler is pessimistic.
- If Events mention untolerated taints, I run `kubectl describe node` and grep for Taints; the fix is either adding a matching toleration or removing the taint.
- If Events mention unbound PVC, I check `kubectl get pvc` and `describe pvc` — usually wrong zone, missing StorageClass, or CSI driver unhealthy.
- If Events mention topology spread or affinity, I check the pod spec's constraints — `DoNotSchedule` spread with tight `maxSkew` is a classic cause during rolling updates.
- If Events mention exceeded quota, `kubectl describe resourcequota` shows used vs hard limits.

**Catching things `describe pod` doesn't tell you**
- If Events are empty after several minutes, the scheduler itself might be unhealthy or a validating admission webhook is blocking — check `kube-scheduler` pod and validatingwebhookconfigurations.
- Nodes auto-taint on NotReady or memory-pressure — if every new pod is Pending with taint reasons cluster-wide, the cluster is unhealthy, not the pod.
- Pod density limits per node on AWS VPC CNI — a t3.small only holds 11 pods, so CPU-free doesn't mean pod-free.

**Preventive patterns I put in place**
- Use VPA in recommend-only mode to right-size requests — oversized requests cause unnecessary Pending.
- PodDisruptionBudget plus minReplicas 2 so rolling updates don't pin a lone pod unable to find a new home.
- PriorityClasses on critical workloads so they preempt lower-priority pods rather than sit Pending.
- Prometheus alert on `kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Pending"} > 5m` — anything Pending more than 5 minutes is an incident.

**Escalation order**
- Single pod Pending → look at the pod's constraints.
- All new pods in one namespace → Quota, StorageClass, default LimitRange.
- All new pods cluster-wide → scheduler health, CNI/CSI driver, node readiness.

questions.question: A Spring Boot pod is in `CrashLoopBackOff` — how do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.title: Debugging `CrashLoopBackOff`: Why Pods Crash and How to Fix Them
questions.direct_answer: `CrashLoopBackOff` means the container started, exited, and kubelet is backing off before the next restart (10s → 20s → 40s → ... up to 5 min). Root causes: (1) **App crashes on startup** — missing config, bad DB creds, port conflict, OOMKilled; (2) **Liveness probe failing** — endpoint doesn't exist or app is slow to warm up; (3) **Init container failing**; (4) **Missing Secret/ConfigMap**. Debug order: `kubectl describe pod` (exit code + reason) → `kubectl logs --previous` (logs of the crashed container) → `kubectl logs -f` if still running → check probes, init containers, and env/secret refs. Exit code 137 = OOMKilled; 143 = SIGTERM.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know to read `--previous` logs, interpret exit codes, and distinguish app crashes from probe failures
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only reading current logs (empty because the container restarted) and missing `--previous`; or confusing probe-induced kills with app crashes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain exit code table (137 OOMKilled, 1 app error, 143 SIGTERM, 139 SIGSEGV), `kubectl debug` ephemeral containers, `terminationMessagePath`, backoff timing, startup probe to prevent liveness-during-warmup kills, and sidecar crashes affecting the main container

sections.title: What `CrashLoopBackOff` Actually Means
sections.content:
`CrashLoopBackOff` is not itself an error — it's kubelet saying "the container keeps exiting; I'm waiting before the next restart." The backoff sequence is **exponential**: 10s → 20s → 40s → 80s → 160s → 300s (capped). Each crash cycle counts toward the pod's restart count; kubelet never gives up, just waits longer.

The hard part of debugging is that by the time you look, the container has already exited. `kubectl logs pod` returns empty or only a few lines from the most recent attempt. **The key flag is `--previous`** — shows logs from the immediately prior terminated container instance, which almost always holds the stack trace or error message.

Four dominant root causes:

1. **App crash on startup.** Bad config, missing DB, port conflict, unhandled exception in `main()`, OOMKilled from too-low memory limit.
2. **Liveness probe killing a slow-starting app.** Spring Boot takes 30–60s to warm; liveness probe runs before then and kubelet SIGKILLs.
3. **Init container failing.** Main container never starts; init's logs hold the reason.
4. **Missing ConfigMap / Secret reference.** The pod mounts a Secret that doesn't exist; container fails to start.

**Exit codes** give immediate signal:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Clean exit (shouldn't loop) |
| 1 | General app error — unhandled exception, failed main |
| 137 | SIGKILL — typically OOMKilled |
| 139 | SIGSEGV — native crash (rare for JVM) |
| 143 | SIGTERM — graceful shutdown requested |
| 2 | Shell misuse, often wrong ENTRYPOINT |

sections.title: The Diagnostic Flow
sections.content:
Read metadata first, then previous logs, then current logs. Branch based on exit reason.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Start[Pod CrashLoopBackOff] --> Desc[kubectl describe pod]
    Desc --> LastState[Last State section\nExit code + Reason]
    LastState -->|ExitCode: 137\nReason: OOMKilled| OOM[OOM path:\ncheck limits, MaxRAMPercentage, heap dump]
    LastState -->|ExitCode: 1\nReason: Error| App[App error path]
    LastState -->|Reason: ContainerCannotRun| Run[Entrypoint/image path]
    LastState -->|Events show Liveness probe failed| Probe[Probe path]
    LastState -->|Init container failed| Init[Init container path]

    App --> PrevLogs[kubectl logs POD --previous]
    PrevLogs --> Trace{Stack trace?}
    Trace -->|Yes| Fix1[Read exception: DB, config, port, etc]
    Trace -->|Logs empty| CCD[kubectl debug with ephemeral container\nOR exec into init shell]

    Probe --> P1[Check livenessProbe spec]
    P1 --> P2{Endpoint / port right?}
    P2 -->|Wrong| P3[Fix probe endpoint]
    P2 -->|Right but app slow to start| P4[Add startupProbe\nOR increase initialDelay]

    Init --> I1[kubectl logs POD -c INIT_NAME --previous]

    OOM --> O1[kubectl describe node | grep Memory]
    O1 --> O2[Raise memory limit OR\nset -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75]
```

Exit code 137 goes to OOM path. Exit code 1 goes to app error path via `--previous` logs. Probe-induced kills show up as events, not exit codes.

sections.title: Step 1: `kubectl describe pod` and Interpret Last State
sections.content:
The describe output tells you WHY the last container died.

```bash
kubectl describe pod order-svc-7d8b-abc -n prod | sed -n '/Containers:/,$p'
# Containers:
#   app:
#     Image:  myregistry/order:1.2.3
#     State:  Waiting
#       Reason: CrashLoopBackOff
#     Last State: Terminated
#       Reason:       Error
#       Exit Code:    1
#       Started:      Tue, 21 Apr 2026 10:14:02
#       Finished:     Tue, 21 Apr 2026 10:14:18
#     Ready:          False
#     Restart Count:  7
# Events:
#   Warning  Unhealthy  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.0.1.5:8080/actuator/health": dial tcp 10.0.1.5:8080: connect: connection refused
#   Normal   Killing    kubelet  Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
```

**Key fields:**

- **`Last State.Reason`** — `Error` (app exit), `OOMKilled` (SIGKILL from cgroup OOM), `ContainerCannotRun` (entrypoint missing / bad image).
- **`Last State.Exit Code`** — decode with table above.
- **`Ready: False`** and **`Restart Count`** climbing — confirms the loop.
- **Events** — may reveal probe failures that triggered the restart.

**Common interpretations:**

- `Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137` — cgroup memory limit hit. Raise `resources.limits.memory`, or tune `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` so JVM respects the container limit.
- `Reason: Error, Exit Code: 1` + probe failure event — app exited on its own; logs will tell why.
- `Reason: ContainerCannotRun` — image or ENTRYPOINT problem; verify image exists and the entrypoint path is correct.
- `Reason: Error, Exit Code: 143` — SIGTERM received; typically from kubelet killing after failed liveness probe.

sections.title: Step 2: `kubectl logs --previous` — The Stack Trace From the Dead Container
sections.content:
Once the container restarts, `kubectl logs` returns the new instance's logs (probably just starting). To see the crashed instance's last output:

```bash
kubectl logs order-svc-7d8b-abc -n prod --previous
# 2026-04-21 10:14:18.723 ERROR 1 --- [main] o.s.boot.SpringApplication :
# Application run failed
# org.springframework.beans.factory.UnsatisfiedDependencyException: ...
#     Caused by: java.sql.SQLException: FATAL: password authentication failed for user "app"
# ...
```

That is the root cause staring at you. **Fix**: the DB password Secret is wrong or missing.

**Common crash patterns and their messages:**

- **DB connection / auth failure** — `Cannot get a connection`, `Connection refused`, `password authentication failed`. Check Secret, ConfigMap, DB availability from pod (`kubectl exec -it pod -- nc -zv db-host 5432`).
- **Missing config property** — `Could not resolve placeholder 'MISSING_PROP'`. Spring Boot config not loaded; check `envFrom` reference or `application.yml` mounted path.
- **Port already in use** — rare but happens with sidecars listening on the same port.
- **Class not found / NoSuchMethodError** — Jib/Dockerfile produced an incomplete classpath.
- **`OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`** — JVM ran out of non-heap memory even before hitting the container limit; increase `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`.

**If `--previous` returns 'previous terminated container not found':** the container has restarted many times, very fast; kubelet may have dropped the previous log. Fixes: check Events history, or temporarily add a `preStop` sleep to slow the loop for inspection.

**Init container logs:**

```bash
kubectl logs POD -n NS -c INIT_NAME --previous
```

Init containers run in order before the main container; a failing init (e.g., waiting for DB to be ready) keeps the pod in `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` with no main container logs at all.

sections.title: Step 3: Liveness Probes Killing Slow-Starting JVMs
sections.content:
A classic Spring Boot scenario: the app takes 45 seconds to start (Spring context, JPA, Kafka clients). Liveness probe is configured with `initialDelaySeconds: 30`, fires on an app that isn't ready, kubelet records 3 failures (at ~30, 40, 50s), kills the container. CrashLoopBackOff begins.

**`describe pod` events show this clearly:**

```
Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
Normal   Killing    Container app failed liveness probe, will be restarted
```

But the app didn't crash — it was SIGKILLed while still warming up.

**Fix: use a startup probe in addition to liveness.**

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}
  failureThreshold: 30    # total 30 * 5s = 150s allowed
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: {path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080}
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
```

`startupProbe` runs until it succeeds once; only then do liveness / readiness begin. This gives slow-starting JVMs 150s of grace without loosening liveness for the rest of the pod's life.

**Common probe mistakes:**

- Hitting `/actuator/health` (aggregate) which includes dependencies; use `/actuator/health/liveness` (Spring Boot 2.3+) that returns UP even if DB is down, so transient DB issues don't kill the pod.
- `initialDelaySeconds` too high hiding real crashes, or too low killing warm-up.
- Liveness and readiness using the same endpoint — during DB outage, both fail, pod restarts pointlessly instead of just being taken out of Service rotation.
- `failureThreshold: 1` on liveness — a single flaky probe kills a healthy pod.

**OOMKilled path (`ExitCode: 137`):**

- Raise `resources.limits.memory`.
- Set JVM flags: `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+UseContainerSupport` (default since JDK 10 but worth verifying).
- Capture heap dump: `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps` with a hostPath or emptyDir for post-mortem.
- Check for memory leaks with `jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info` or a profiler.

sections.title: Ephemeral Containers, Init Failures, and Production Hardening
sections.content:
**`kubectl debug` with ephemeral containers.** When the crashed pod has no shell or you need to inspect the filesystem:

```bash
kubectl debug -it order-svc-... --image=busybox --target=app -n prod
# attach a busybox sidecar sharing process namespace with 'app'
ps aux
cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n'
ls /config
```

The ephemeral container shares PID and filesystem namespaces so you can see the main container's environment and config without rebuilding the image.

**`terminationMessagePath`.** A container can write its cause-of-death to `/dev/termination-log` (default); kubelet surfaces it as `Last State.Message`. For Spring Boot, configure a `@PreDestroy` or `SpringApplication.exit()` handler that writes the last error to the termination log — this puts the root cause in `describe pod` output without even reading logs.

**Sidecar crashes affecting the main container.** Istio/Envoy/Cilium sidecar that crashes can break the main container's networking. `describe pod` shows each container's state — if the sidecar is `CrashLoopBackOff` and the app is `Ready: False`, fix the sidecar first. In Kubernetes 1.29+, native sidecar containers (`restartPolicy: Always` on init containers) change the ordering so sidecar readiness gates app startup.

**Production hardening:**

- **Structured logs to stdout** — so `kubectl logs` gives immediate signal; don't log only to a file.
- **Spring Boot `spring.main.banner-mode=off`** + **`logging.pattern.console`** for concise pod-friendly output.
- **Startup probe on every JVM service** — eliminates warm-up kills permanently.
- **Readiness probe tied to DB health checks conservatively** — if DB is down briefly, pod drops from Service rotation but doesn't restart; when DB returns, pod returns to rotation without cold start.
- **Alert on `kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total` rate** — restart rate > 0 per 10 min is a signal before users notice.
- **`restartPolicy: OnFailure` for Jobs**, not Deployments — Deployments should not have custom restart policy (only `Always` is valid).
- **Resource limits = requests for critical services** — no burst, predictable; prevents CPU throttling confusion during diagnosis.
- **Always capture heap dumps on OOMKill** — `emptyDir` or `hostPath` volume at `/dumps`, then copy out with `kubectl cp` before the pod is replaced.

**Escalation pattern:**

1. One pod — app bug, config typo, probe misconfig.
2. All pods of a Deployment — bad image, wrong Secret, env misconfig.
3. Many Deployments crashing simultaneously — node issue, cluster-wide DNS failure, or platform-level problem (CoreDNS, cert-manager, Istio control plane).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CrashLoopBackOff is a backoff status, not an error** — kubelet is waiting before restart; exponential 10s → 300s.
- **`kubectl logs --previous` is the primary tool** — shows the crashed container's last output; without it you see only the new attempt.
- **Exit code table:** 137 = OOMKilled, 1 = app error, 143 = SIGTERM, 139 = SIGSEGV, 2 = ENTRYPOINT issue.
- **Liveness probe on a slow-starting JVM causes crash loops** — add a startupProbe so liveness doesn't fire during warm-up.
- **Use `/actuator/health/liveness`, not aggregate `/actuator/health`** — so transient DB outage doesn't restart the pod.
- **Init container failure keeps pod in `Init:CrashLoopBackOff`** — check init logs specifically with `-c INIT_NAME --previous`.
- **`kubectl debug` ephemeral containers** — attach a busybox to inspect filesystem and env without rebuilding the image.
- **Sidecar crashes can mask main-container health** — check all containers in the pod; Kubernetes 1.29+ native sidecars fix ordering.
- **`terminationMessagePath`** surfaces root cause in `describe pod` — write last error there for immediate diagnosis.
- **Capture heap dumps on OOMKill** before the pod is replaced — `emptyDir` at /dumps + `kubectl cp`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting and kubelet is waiting before the next restart with exponential backoff from 10 seconds up to 5 minutes. The symptom is a loop; the root cause is one of a handful of things.

**The diagnostic flow I use**
- `kubectl describe pod` and read the Last State section — that gives the exit code and reason. 137 means OOMKilled, 1 is an app error, 143 is SIGTERM, 2 is an ENTRYPOINT issue.
- `kubectl logs POD --previous` — this is the critical step most people miss. The current container just started so `kubectl logs` returns almost nothing; `--previous` shows the last crashed container's output which usually has the stack trace.
- Check the Events section for liveness probe failures — if the probe is killing the pod during startup, the app didn't crash, it was SIGKILLed.

**The big four root causes**
- App crash on startup — bad DB credentials, missing config, port conflict. Fix via logs: "password authentication failed" or "Could not resolve placeholder".
- Liveness probe killing a slow-starting JVM — Spring Boot takes 30 to 60 seconds to warm up; liveness fires before then, kubelet SIGKILLs. Fix: add a startupProbe so liveness only starts after startup succeeds once.
- Init container failing — pod shows `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` and main container never starts. Check init logs with `-c INIT_NAME --previous`.
- OOMKilled (exit code 137) — cgroup memory limit hit. Raise memory limit and set `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75` so JVM respects the container limit.

**Probe configuration**
- Use `/actuator/health/liveness` from Spring Boot 2.3+, not aggregate `/actuator/health` — the liveness endpoint returns UP even if DB is temporarily down, so transient DB issues don't cause pointless restarts.
- startupProbe plus livenessProbe plus readinessProbe is the production pattern — startup covers warm-up, liveness restarts on true hangs, readiness takes the pod out of Service rotation during transient issues.

**Tools that help when logs aren't enough**
- `kubectl debug --image=busybox --target=CONTAINER` attaches an ephemeral container sharing process and filesystem namespace — you can inspect /proc, environment, mounted configs without rebuilding the image.
- `terminationMessagePath` lets the container write its cause-of-death; kubelet surfaces it in `describe pod`, so root cause is visible even if logs were lost.

**Escalation pattern**
- One pod — app bug, config typo, probe misconfig.
- All pods of one Deployment — bad image, wrong Secret, env misconfig.
- Many Deployments — node issue, DNS failure cluster-wide, or platform-level problem.

**Production hardening I apply**
- Startup probe on every JVM service.
- `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` writing to an emptyDir at /dumps so I can copy the dump out before the pod is replaced.
- Prometheus alert on restart rate per 10 minutes — catches CrashLoop before users notice.

questions.question: Services in the cluster suddenly fail DNS resolution — how do you debug CoreDNS?
questions.title: Debugging CoreDNS: When Kubernetes Service DNS Fails
questions.direct_answer: CoreDNS runs as a Deployment in `kube-system` resolving `*.svc.cluster.local` for all pods. DNS failures usually manifest as `UnknownHostException` or random 50% failures (one CoreDNS pod unhealthy). Debug order: (1) `kubectl exec pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default` to verify DNS from a pod; (2) check CoreDNS pods healthy (`kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns`); (3) check CoreDNS logs for errors; (4) validate `/etc/resolv.conf` in pod (correct nameserver + search domains); (5) check NetworkPolicy isn't blocking DNS (UDP/53 to kube-dns); (6) verify CoreDNS ConfigMap. Fix: scale CoreDNS replicas, enable NodeLocal DNSCache, tune pod `ndots`, check for upstream resolver issues.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know that DNS is the most common intermittent-failure culprit and how to isolate it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming 'service is unreachable' means networking broken, without checking DNS first; or restarting CoreDNS pods without reading logs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain `ndots: 5`, search domain expansion, NodeLocal DNSCache for scalability, NetworkPolicy egress rules for DNS, CoreDNS Corefile plugins, and the classic DNS intermittency caused by conntrack race on parallel DNS queries

sections.title: Why DNS Is the First Thing to Check When 'Networking Is Broken'
sections.content:
In a Kubernetes cluster, every service call that uses a service name (`payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local`) depends on DNS working. **CoreDNS** (replaced kube-dns in 1.13+) is the in-cluster resolver — a Deployment of 2–3 pods in `kube-system` that every pod queries via a ClusterIP Service (typically `kube-dns` at `10.96.0.10`).

CoreDNS handles:

- Cluster-internal names (`*.svc.cluster.local`, `*.pod.cluster.local`) resolved from the Kubernetes API.
- External names forwarded to upstream resolvers (cloud VPC DNS or `/etc/resolv.conf` of the node).
- Custom rewrites and stub zones defined in the **Corefile** (CoreDNS ConfigMap).

Symptoms of DNS failure range from obvious (all service-to-service calls break with `UnknownHostException`) to insidious:

- **Intermittent ~5% failure rate** — one of 3 CoreDNS pods is unhealthy, queries landed on it fail.
- **50% failure on specific services** — only external DNS broken (upstream resolver issue), cluster-internal still works.
- **First query always slow (5s), subsequent fast** — `ndots: 5` + `search` list causes parallel A/AAAA query race triggering conntrack bugs (classic Linux kernel issue).
- **Pod can't reach DB despite DB being up** — NetworkPolicy blocking egress to kube-dns on UDP/53.

Rule of thumb: **before concluding a service is down, prove DNS resolves its name**. It saves hours of wrong-path debugging.

sections.title: The DNS Resolution Path for a Spring Boot Pod
sections.content:
App calls `payment-service` → glibc queries `/etc/resolv.conf` nameserver → kube-proxy routes to CoreDNS pod → CoreDNS answers from Kubernetes API or upstream.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    App[Spring Boot Pod\nInetAddress.getByName payment-service] --> Resolv[/etc/resolv.conf\nnameserver 10.96.0.10\nsearch ns.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local\noptions ndots:5]
    Resolv -->|UDP/53 to 10.96.0.10| KDS[kube-dns Service\nClusterIP]
    KDS -->|kube-proxy iptables| CD1[CoreDNS Pod 1]
    KDS --> CD2[CoreDNS Pod 2]
    CD1 -->|cluster zone match| K8sAPI[Kubernetes API\nServices + Endpoints]
    CD1 -->|external query| Upstream[Upstream DNS\nVPC resolver / 8.8.8.8]
    CD1 -.failing.-> X[Errors surface\nas UnknownHostException\nor timeout]
    NLC[NodeLocal DNSCache\nDaemonSet on each node] -.optional cache.-> CD1
    NP[NetworkPolicy egress\nmust allow UDP/53 to kube-dns] -.blocks if misconfigured.-> KDS
```

**`ndots: 5` behavior:** if the query has fewer than 5 dots, glibc appends the search list and tries each — so `payment-service` becomes `payment-service.ns.svc.cluster.local`, `payment-service.svc.cluster.local`, `payment-service.cluster.local`, and finally `payment-service` itself. External DNS like `google.com` (1 dot) also goes through this expansion — multiple queries per lookup, each doing parallel A + AAAA.

sections.title: Step 1: Verify DNS From a Pod — The One Command That Answers Everything
sections.content:
The fastest diagnosis is to run nslookup from inside an affected pod.

```bash
# Spawn a debug pod if the affected app has no shell
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sh
# Inside the pod:
nslookup kubernetes.default
# Server:    10.96.0.10
# Name:      kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
# Address:   10.96.0.1

nslookup payment-service.prod.svc.cluster.local
# success or failure tells you if CoreDNS resolves THIS name

nslookup google.com
# tests external resolution via upstream

cat /etc/resolv.conf
# nameserver 10.96.0.10
# search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
# options ndots:5
```

**Interpretation:**

| Result | Diagnosis |
|---|---|
| `kubernetes.default` fails | DNS totally broken — CoreDNS down or unreachable (NetworkPolicy / kube-proxy / iptables). |
| Internal name fails, external works | Service doesn't exist, wrong namespace, or label mismatch on Service — check `kubectl get svc`. |
| External fails, internal works | Upstream resolver issue — check CoreDNS Corefile `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` or VPC DNS. |
| Intermittent (50% failure on retries) | One CoreDNS pod unhealthy; check `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns`. |
| Resolves but takes 5 seconds | `ndots: 5` + parallel A/AAAA conntrack race — see NodeLocal DNSCache fix. |

**Check CoreDNS health:**

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
# NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
# coredns-74ff55c5b-abc      1/1     Running   0
# coredns-74ff55c5b-xyz      0/1     CrashLoopBackOff  4

kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-74ff55c5b-xyz --previous
# reveals the crash reason — often bad Corefile or upstream timeout loop

kubectl top pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
# CoreDNS pod pegged at 100% CPU = overloaded; scale up replicas
```

sections.title: Step 2: The Corefile, NodeLocal DNSCache, and ndots Tuning
sections.content:
**CoreDNS Corefile** is a ConfigMap in `kube-system`:

```bash
kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml
# data:
#   Corefile: |
#     .:53 {
#         errors
#         health { lameduck 5s }
#         ready
#         kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
#            pods insecure
#            fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
#            ttl 30
#         }
#         prometheus :9153
#         forward . /etc/resolv.conf {
#            max_concurrent 1000
#         }
#         cache 30
#         loop
#         reload
#         loadbalance
#     }
```

Common Corefile tweaks:

- **`cache 30`** — CoreDNS caches answers for 30s; tune up for latency or down for consistency.
- **`forward . 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1`** — force a specific upstream instead of inheriting node's resolv.conf; useful when node DNS is broken.
- **`rewrite name substring prod.svc.example.com prod.svc.cluster.local`** — alias externally-looking names to internal.
- **`hosts`** plugin for adding static entries (hotfix for bad external DNS).

**NodeLocal DNSCache** — a DaemonSet on each node running a local CoreDNS cache that pods query first (at a link-local IP). Dramatically reduces query volume hitting CoreDNS pods and eliminates the UDP conntrack race:

```yaml
# Pods' resolv.conf points to 169.254.20.10 (link-local)
# NodeLocal DNSCache pod on each node handles lookups
# Falls back to CoreDNS service for cache misses
```

Standard recommendation for **clusters with >100 nodes or DNS-intensive workloads**. Measurable latency improvement (P99 DNS drops from ~10ms to <1ms) and eliminates the classic 5-second timeout from conntrack collisions.

**ndots tuning.** Pods default to `ndots: 5`. For external-heavy workloads, lower to reduce search expansion:

```yaml
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - name: ndots
        value: "2"
```

With ndots 2, `google.com` is queried once without expansion; internal names like `my-svc` still expand through search list. Cuts external DNS query count by ~5x.

sections.title: Step 3: NetworkPolicy, Overloaded CoreDNS, and External Resolver Failures
sections.content:
**NetworkPolicy blocking DNS.** A strict `default-deny` egress policy that doesn't explicitly allow DNS to `kube-system` will break every pod's name resolution.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-dns, namespace: prod}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}
          podSelector:
            matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53
```

Without this, pods in `prod` with default-deny egress will get `Temporary failure in name resolution`. Debug: compare `kubectl exec` nslookup from a pod in the affected namespace vs one without policy.

**Overloaded CoreDNS.** CoreDNS pod CPU pegged at 100% means queries are queueing. Symptoms: rising DNS latency, occasional timeouts.

Fixes (in order):

1. **Scale CoreDNS replicas**: `kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=5`.
2. **Enable NodeLocal DNSCache** (offloads most queries to per-node cache).
3. **Tune pod `ndots` down** to reduce search expansion multiplier.
4. **Lower cache TTL on upstream if stale data is tolerable** — `cache 60` reduces upstream traffic.
5. **CoreDNS autoscaler** (addon) that scales based on cluster size.

**External resolver failures.** `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` inherits the node's DNS. If the node's VPC DNS (AWS `.2` of the VPC CIDR, GCP metadata server) is unreliable, every external lookup suffers.

Diagnosis:

```bash
kubectl exec coredns-pod -n kube-system -- nslookup google.com
# If this fails, upstream is the issue

kubectl debug node/NODENAME -it --image=busybox
# Then from node context:
nslookup google.com
# Test node-level DNS directly
```

Fixes: switch CoreDNS to `forward . 8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1` explicitly, or fix the VPC / on-prem DNS.

**The classic 5-second DNS timeout.** Linux's glibc sends A and AAAA queries in parallel on the same UDP socket. Conntrack can race, drop one, and retransmit after 5s. Workarounds:

- **NodeLocal DNSCache** uses TCP or dedicated connections.
- **`use-vc`** resolv.conf option (Alpine doesn't support).
- **`single-request-reopen`** — sends A then AAAA on separate sockets.

```yaml
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - {name: single-request-reopen}
      - {name: ndots, value: "2"}
```

sections.title: Production Playbook and Alerting
sections.content:
**15-second triage:**

```bash
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \
  nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl top pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50 | grep -iE 'error|timeout'
```

**Deeper dive:**

```bash
kubectl exec -it affected-pod -n prod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl exec -it affected-pod -n prod -- nslookup payment-service
kubectl get networkpolicy -n prod                    # any deny-egress?
kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml # Corefile review
kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns -o yaml      # check Service is healthy
kubectl get endpoints -n kube-system kube-dns        # does Service have endpoints?
```

**Essential alerts:**

- `coredns_cache_hits_total` vs `coredns_cache_misses_total` ratio — sudden drop = upstream failures.
- `coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds` P99 > 100ms for 5m — CoreDNS overloaded.
- `coredns_panics_total` > 0 — code bug.
- `up{job="kube-dns"}` < 2 — less than 2 CoreDNS pods ready — scale or investigate.
- Pod-level: synthetic probe from a canary pod doing nslookup every 15s; page if failure rate > 1%.

**Production hardening:**

- **Always run ≥ 3 CoreDNS replicas** with topology spread across zones; PDB `minAvailable: 2`.
- **Enable NodeLocal DNSCache** for clusters ≥ 100 nodes or DNS-intensive workloads.
- **Explicit NetworkPolicy allow rule** for DNS egress in every namespace that uses default-deny.
- **Lower pod `ndots` to 2** for external-heavy services.
- **Set pod `single-request-reopen`** for Spring Boot / glibc-based containers.
- **Monitor CoreDNS CPU** — scale early; CoreDNS is a single-CPU-bound resolver per pod.
- **Cache-only pods for critical paths** — some SREs deploy per-app dnsmasq sidecars for mission-critical paths (mostly made obsolete by NodeLocal DNSCache).
- **Document the DNS runbook** — this is the highest-ROI runbook because DNS-induced incidents are both frequent and misdiagnosed.

**The classic production story.** A strict NetworkPolicy is rolled out to prod at 10 AM. At 10:02 AM, all services in `prod` start failing to resolve each other. Only the SREs with the DNS runbook realize within minutes that the default-deny-egress policy doesn't whitelist UDP/53 to kube-dns. A teams without this knowledge chase service health for hours. DNS is always the first thing to check.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **DNS is the most common hidden cause of 'networking is broken'** — always verify with `nslookup kubernetes.default` from an affected pod before anything else.
- **CoreDNS Deployment in `kube-system`** resolves `*.svc.cluster.local` via Kubernetes API and forwards external to upstream.
- **`ndots: 5` + search list causes query amplification** — lower to 2 for external-heavy services; cuts external query count by ~5x.
- **NodeLocal DNSCache is the standard scalability fix** — DaemonSet per node with local cache; eliminates the 5-second conntrack race and cuts CoreDNS load by 10x.
- **NetworkPolicy must allow DNS explicitly** — default-deny egress without a rule for UDP/53 to kube-dns breaks every pod in the namespace.
- **CoreDNS CPU pegs at 100% under load** — scale replicas, enable NodeLocal DNSCache, tune ndots; CoreDNS autoscaler addon for large clusters.
- **Upstream resolver failures surface as 'external fails, internal works'** — CoreDNS inherits node DNS; switch to explicit `forward . 8.8.8.8` or fix VPC DNS.
- **Exit code and logs from CoreDNS pods reveal Corefile bugs** — `kubectl logs` and `kubectl get configmap coredns` for Corefile review.
- **Run ≥ 3 CoreDNS replicas with PDB and topology spread** — losing 2 at once is an outage; spread across AZs for availability.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When I see 'networking seems broken' my first instinct is to verify DNS. In a Kubernetes cluster DNS is responsible for every service name resolution, and intermittent DNS issues are the single most common hidden cause of vague connectivity problems.

**My first command**
- `kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default`.
- If that fails, DNS is totally broken — CoreDNS down or unreachable; check kube-system pods and NetworkPolicy.
- If kubernetes.default works but my service name fails, it's a missing Service, wrong namespace, or label mismatch — `kubectl get svc` and `describe` it.
- If internal works but external doesn't, it's an upstream resolver issue — CoreDNS inherits the node's resolv.conf by default; check the VPC DNS or force an explicit upstream in the Corefile.

**Check CoreDNS health**
- `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns` — any CrashLoopBackOff? Any pod at 100% CPU under load?
- `kubectl logs` on CoreDNS pods with `--previous` if they've restarted — Corefile errors show up here.
- Scale CoreDNS replicas immediately if CPU is pegged — `kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=5`.

**The classic Kubernetes DNS performance issues**
- `ndots: 5` default — every lookup with fewer than 5 dots goes through the search list, so `google.com` becomes 4 queries. Lower ndots to 2 via pod dnsConfig for external-heavy services; cuts external DNS volume 5x.
- The 5-second timeout — glibc sends A and AAAA in parallel on the same UDP socket and conntrack can race, dropping one and retransmitting after 5 seconds. Fixes are `single-request-reopen` in pod dnsConfig or enabling NodeLocal DNSCache which uses TCP.
- NodeLocal DNSCache is the standard scalability answer — a DaemonSet runs on every node with a local cache; pods hit the local cache first, CoreDNS sees only cache misses. Dramatically cuts load and eliminates conntrack races. Standard recommendation for clusters over 100 nodes.

**NetworkPolicy is the production trap**
- A strict default-deny egress policy without an explicit allow rule for UDP/53 to kube-dns breaks every pod in the namespace.
- The rule must allow both UDP and TCP port 53 to pods labeled `k8s-app: kube-dns` in `kube-system`.
- Classic production incident: a security-hardening policy rolls out, all services start failing to resolve, the fix is a one-line NetworkPolicy addition but it takes hours to find without the runbook.

**Essential alerting I put in place**
- CoreDNS P99 request duration > 100ms for 5 minutes — CoreDNS is overloaded.
- CoreDNS cache hit ratio drops suddenly — upstream failures.
- At least 2 CoreDNS pods ready — less than 2 is an incident.
- A synthetic DNS probe pod doing nslookup every 15 seconds — page at >1% failure rate.

**Production hardening**
- At least 3 CoreDNS replicas with topology spread across AZs and PDB minAvailable 2.
- NodeLocal DNSCache enabled.
- Pod-level ndots and single-request-reopen tuning.
- Explicit NetworkPolicy allow-dns rule in every namespace that uses default-deny.
- Document the DNS runbook — this is the single highest-ROI runbook because DNS-induced incidents are frequent and misdiagnosed.

beats.text: In a Kubernetes cluster, every service call that uses a service name (payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local) depends on DNS working. CoreDNS (replaced kube-dns in 1.13+) is the in-cluster resolver — a Deployment of 2–3 pods in kube-system that every pod queries via a ClusterIP Service (typically kube-dns at 10.96.0.10). CoreDNS handles: Cluster-internal names.
Whether you know that DNS is the most common intermittent-failure culprit and how to isolate it

steps: The fastest diagnosis is to run nslookup from inside an affected pod.

``bash Spawn a debug pod if the affected app has no shell kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sh Inside the pod: nslookup kubernetes.default Server: 10.96.0.10 Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local Address: 10.96.0.1 nslookup payment-service.prod.svc.cluster.local success or failure tells you if CoreDNS resolves THIS name nslookup google.com tests external resolution via upstream cat /etc/resolv.conf nameserver 10.96.0.10 search prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local options ndots:5 ` Interpretation: | Result | Diagnosis | |---|---| | kubernetes.default fails | DNS totally broken — CoreDNS down or unreachable (NetworkPolicy / kube-proxy / iptables).
| | Internal name fails, external works | Service doesn't exist, wrong namespace, or label mismatch on Service — check kubectl get svc.
| | External fails, internal works | Upstream resolver issue — check CoreDNS Corefile forward .
| | Intermittent (50% failure on retries) | One CoreDNS pod unhealthy; check kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns.
